title: What competence and training does Japan's medical device QMS ordinance require?
description: Japan's QMS Ordinance (MHLW Ordinance No. 169 of 2004) Articles 22 and 23: competence, training, effectiveness checks, awareness and five-year records.
shortAnswer: Japan's QMS Ordinance (MHLW Ordinance No. 169 of 2004) requires medical device and in vitro diagnostic marketing authorization holders, and their registered manufacturing sites, to define the competence needed for work affecting product quality, provide training or other action to achieve and maintain it, evaluate its effectiveness, make staff aware of their contribution to quality objectives, and keep training records for five years (Articles 22, 23, 67 and 68).
keyTakeaways: Article 22 requires everyone whose work affects product quality to have the necessary competence based on appropriate education and training, skills and experience, and requires a documented process for training and awareness.

Article 23 has five duties: define the competence needed, provide training or other action to acquire or maintain it, evaluate the effectiveness of that action, ensure awareness of quality objectives, and keep records of education, training, skills and experience.
MHLW Ordinance No. 60 of 2021 added the documented process requirement and the duty to maintain competence; its three-year transitional period ended in March 2024.
Extra training duties apply to staff working temporarily in special work environments (Article 25(4)), biological devices (Article 77) and reprocessed single-use devices (Article 81-2-4).
Training documents and records are kept for five years, even where product records run 15 years or longer (Articles 67 and 68).
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), with the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA), registered certification bodies and prefectures conducting QMS conformity inspections
appliesTo: Marketing authorization holders (seizō hanbaigyōsha) for medical devices and in vitro diagnostics
Foreign special approval holders and foreign designated highly controlled device manufacturers
Registered manufacturing sites (tōroku seizōsho) in Japan and abroad, through Article 83
Top management, management representatives, domestic quality operations responsible persons and all staff whose work affects product quality

sections.heading: Where does the QMS training duty come from?

blocks.text: The duty sits in the **Ministerial Ordinance on Standards for Manufacturing Control and Quality Control of Medical Devices and In Vitro Diagnostics** (医療機器及び体外診断用医薬品の製造管理及び品質管理の基準に関する省令, MHLW Ordinance No. 169 of 2004), known as the QMS Ordinance. Article 1 says it sets the standards referred to in Article 23-2-5(2)(iv) and Article 80(2) of the PMD Act (Act No. 145 of 1960) ([QMS Ordinance, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/416M60000100169)).

Under Article 23-2-5(2)(iv) of the PMD Act, approval of a device or in vitro diagnostic designated by Cabinet Order is refused where its manufacturing control or quality control method is not found to conform to that standard. Article 23-2-5(6) requires a document or on-site QMS conformity inspection at approval and again after each period set by Cabinet Order, which may not be shorter than three years ([PMD Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/335AC0000000145)). Competence and training records are standard inspection evidence.

Readers who work with ISO 13485 will recognize the structure: a quality management monitoring system (hinshitsu kanri kantoku shisutemu), top management responsibility, resource management, product realization and measurement. Competence and training sit in Section 4 of Chapter 2, resource management.

Article 22 (competence of quality work personnel) sets the outcome and the process. Paragraph 1 requires the MAH to ensure that everyone engaged in work affecting product quality has the competence needed for the work, based on appropriate education and training, skills and experience. Paragraph 2 requires the MAH to document its process for providing appropriate training to personnel and for ensuring they are aware of the work that affects product quality.
Article 23 (competence, awareness and education and training) then lists five duties:

items: determine what competence is needed by people engaged in work affecting product quality;
provide education and training or take other action so they acquire or maintain that competence;
evaluate the effectiveness of that action;
ensure that every member of staff understands the meaning and importance of their own work and how they contribute to achieving quality objectives; and
create and keep appropriate records of personnel's education, training, skills and experience.

blocks.text: Item 3, the effectiveness evaluation, does not apply to limited Type 3 MAHs (gentei daisanshu iryō kiki seizō hanbaigyōsha), which handle only certain general medical devices. Everything else applies to them.
MHLW Ordinance No. 60 of 2021, promulgated and in force March 26, 2021, revised the QMS Ordinance. Comparing the e-Gov versions before and after, three changes affect training:

blocks.text: Article 2 of the 2021 supplementary provisions allowed MAHs to keep following the previous rules until three years had passed from entry into force, so the revised text became fully binding in March 2024. The word "maintain" matters: it turns training into a recurring duty, so a one-off onboarding record no longer shows conformity for long-serving staff.

Looking ahead, MHLW Ordinance No. 142 of 2026 amends the QMS Ordinance from May 20, 2027, but comparing versions on e-Gov, Articles 22 and 23 are unchanged. As at November 2026 the training text in force is the 2021 text.

sections.heading: Which work needs extra training beyond Article 23?

blocks.text: Three provisions add specific training on top of the general duty.

items: **Special work environments (Article 25(4)):** everyone required to work temporarily under special work environment conditions, such as a cleanroom, must receive the Article 23(ii) training and have the competence needed, unless they are supervised by staff who have.

**Biological devices (Article 77):** MAHs handling biological devices must document procedures to train staff in manufacturing or testing in microbiology, medicine, veterinary medicine and related subjects, and to train staff working in aseptic areas or areas handling pathogenic microorganisms in measures to prevent microbial contamination, keeping records.

**Reprocessed single-use devices (Article 81-2-4):** MAHs handling reprocessed single-use devices must document procedures for training staff in manufacturing or testing in microbiology, medicine, veterinary medicine and related subjects, and keep records.

blocks.text: Role requirements also have a competence element. Article 72 requires the domestic quality operations responsible person (kokunai hinshitsu gyōmu un'ei sekininsha) to head the quality assurance unit, to have at least three years in quality control or similar work and not to belong to a sales department.

sections.heading: Do registered manufacturing sites have the same training duty?

blocks.text: Yes. Article 83 applies Chapters 2 to 5-2 of the ordinance, including Articles 22 and 23, to the manufacturer of a registered manufacturing site that performs outsourced processes for an MAH or supplies purchased items to it, with limited exclusions. A site may exclude provisions that are not appropriate for the processes it performs, but must state the exclusion in its quality manual. Article 84 then requires the MAH to confirm that registered sites manage their own outsourcing and suppliers properly, which in practice includes checking their training records during supplier audits.

sections.heading: How long must QMS training records be kept?

blocks.text: Five years. Article 68 requires records to be kept for 15 years from creation for specially maintained medical devices and five years for other products, each extended to the expiry period plus one year where longer, but sets five years for records relating to education and training. Article 67 applies the same five-year rule to training documents. Articles 77(2) and 78 apply five years to biological device training records even though other biological device records run to the expiry period plus 10 or 30 years. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

blocks.text: The effectiveness row is where inspections most often probe. [How to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator) sets out methods that fit Article 23(iii).

sections.heading: What happens if training does not meet the QMS Ordinance?

blocks.text: A training nonconformity is a QMS nonconformity. It can delay approval where found at the pre-approval inspection, and after approval Article 72(2) of the PMD Act lets the Minister order an MAH whose manufacturing control or quality control method does not conform to the QMS standard to improve it, or to suspend business until it does. Because Article 23-2-5(6) inspections recur, gaps found once tend to be checked again at the next inspection.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Articles 22, 23, 25, 77 and 81-2-4 as obligations linked to the MAH's procedures and role profiles, then defines the competence, learning outcomes and assessment points for each role before content is written. Effectiveness evidence is captured against the same competence definitions, so Article 23(iii) has a traceable record.

faqs.q: Does the QMS Ordinance set a minimum training frequency?
faqs.a: No. Article 23 requires training to acquire or maintain competence and an evaluation of its effectiveness, but no interval. MAHs set refresher frequency in their documented training process under Article 22(2), usually by role risk, procedure changes and effectiveness results.

faqs.q: Are foreign manufacturing sites covered by the QMS training articles?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are registered manufacturing sites that perform processes for a Japanese MAH. Article 83 applies Chapters 2 to 5-2, including Articles 22 and 23, to manufacturers of registered sites, which include foreign manufacturers registered under the PMD Act.

faqs.q: What is a limited Type 3 MAH, and what does it skip?
faqs.a: A limited Type 3 medical device MAH handles only certain general medical devices. Article 23 exempts it from item 3, the evaluation of training effectiveness. It must still define competence, provide training, ensure awareness and keep records.

faqs.q: Do QMS training records have to be kept as long as device history records?
faqs.a: No. Articles 67 and 68 set five years for documents and records relating to education and training, even where other records for specially maintained devices must be kept 15 years or for the expiry period plus one year.
